messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Train Conductor
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir, a 29-year-old train conductor, still remembers the precise temperature of that February afternoon—the way the air bit at his cheeks as he leaned out of the cab, and then, seconds later, the shocking cold of the young woman’s skin when he knelt beside her on the gravel. She had stepped onto the tracks just before the express curve, and by the time Amir saw her, the train was already past the point of braking. The impact threw her clear of the wheels, but the damage was done. When he reached her, blood was pooling beneath her head, dark and thick against the white stones. Her left arm was bent at an angle he knew was wrong. He touched her wrist to check for a pulse and felt only the damp chill of her skin, already cooling in the wind. She was gone before the ambulance arrived.

In the weeks that followed, Amir tried to tell himself it was over. The investigation cleared him of any fault. His supervisor said, “You did everything right.” His coworkers clapped his shoulder and told him to go home and rest. But Amir found that no amount of reassurance could quiet the feeling that the world was not safe—that at any moment, something terrible could happen again, and this time it might be his fault because he had not seen it coming soon enough. He began to scan the tracks obsessively, his eyes darting from rail to rail, checking for shadows or figures. Even when the train was stopped at a station, he would catch himself listening for a sound that did not belong, straining for a scream or a thud that never came. The hypervigilance followed him off the job. At night, lying in his apartment, he kept his bedroom door open so he could hear the street. He convinced himself that he needed to stay alert, that the moment he let his guard down would be the moment something went wrong. Sleep came only in shallow, fitful stretches after the streetlights dimmed and the last car passed.

The triggers were everywhere, and they felt as if they were designed to ambush him. A sudden chill on his skin—from an air conditioner, or the handle of a cold drink—would pull his mind back to that gravel bed and the feel of her wrist. Blood was the worst. Once, a passenger on the train cut his hand on a broken window latch, and Amir saw the red streak across the man’s palm. He had to lock himself in the crew restroom for ten minutes, hands shaking, until the image of that earlier blood faded. Visible injuries on others—a child’s scraped knee, a commuter’s bandaged arm—made his stomach clench and his chest tighten. He started avoiding eye contact with passengers, especially during the evening rush when people were tired and more likely to have minor wounds or patches on their skin. His boss noticed that Amir had become jumpy, that he double-checked doors and brakes long after they were secure. “You’re fine,” the boss said. “The system is safe.” But Amir did not believe it. Safety, for him, had become a word that meant nothing unless he could see, hear, and feel every possible danger for himself.

The social cost crept up slowly. He stopped going out with friends, because at a bar the sight of a napkin stained red from someone’s salsa would spike his heart rate. He avoided his sister’s house because her toddler had a habit of scraping his knees and showing off the scabs. He told himself it was easier to stay home, where he could control the temperature, the lighting, the level of threat. But home wasn’t safe either; it was just less unpredictable. He spent most evenings pacing his apartment, checking the locks twice, then lying on his bed with his eyes open, listening.

Amir finally decided to seek help after an incident three weeks ago. During a routine inspection, he found a small puddle of coolant under one of the train cars—it had a film of red hydraulic fluid, and the sight of that oily red on the concrete sent him into a full panic attack. He could not breathe, could not think, could not move until another conductor pulled him away. That night, he realized he could not go on like this. He made an appointment with a therapist who specialized in trauma. Sitting in the waiting room, he held his hands tightly in his lap and thought about what he wanted most: to feel, even for a minute, as if the world were not a place where danger was hiding around every corner. But he was also afraid—afraid that if he let himself believe he was safe, he would stop being watchful enough to keep everyone else alive.
